title: Show your work
lede: Orbitz was one product of a small Canadian company, so the record is thin: a handful of contemporary articles, the company’s own statements to the trade press, and its later SEC filings. This entry is shorter than most for that reason. Every link was opened while this page was researched.

notes.label: Company claims
notes.text: The million cases by the end of 1996 is the company’s own forecast-style claim, reported by AP in October 1996, not an audited figure.[^1]

notes.label: Conflicts
notes.text: The Washington Post article is dated April 20, 1997 on its page and April 21 in its web address.[^3] Atlas Obscura says Orbitz launched and sold through Orbitz.com in 1996 and was discontinued by 1999; we have no exact date for the last production.[^5]

notes.label: Unknown
notes.text: Total Orbitz sales over its life; the exact discontinuation date; whether the Strategy figures are US or Canadian dollars. Clearly Canadian’s pre-2002 annual reports were filed on paper and are not on EDGAR.

notes.label: Videos
notes.text: No Orbitz television commercial could be found, consistent with the company’s no-advertising approach.[^4] The other videos are embedded as commentary.

notes.label: Images
notes.text: Both photographs are from Wikimedia Commons under the licences in their credits. Swatches are approximations. The drawing is original.

notes.label: Revenue bases
notes.text: Revenue for 1998 to 2002 is from the annual report for 2002; later years are the first figures printed for each year. Later reports restated 2002, 2004 and 2005, and from 2006 sales incentives are netted against sales, so the series is not on one basis. Clearly Canadian reports in US dollars under Canadian accounting rules.[^6][^15][^16][^17][^18][^19]

notes.label: Share prices
notes.text: High and low prices are US-dollar quotations from the annual reports, on Nasdaq and the OTC Bulletin Board. OTC quotations are inter-dealer prices and may not match actual sales. The annual reports do not adjust the 1998 and 1999 prices for the February 18, 1999 consolidation of 4.25 old shares into 1 new share.[^6]

notes.label: Derived
notes.text: That Hansen Natural’s net sales rose in every year from 1998 to 2002 is read from the five annual figures in its annual report for 2002. Its net sales and Clearly Canadian’s total revenues are defined differently, and no percentage is computed.[^6][^20]

notes.label: Secondary sources
notes.text: FundingUniverse (sources 13 and 14) is a reference work. Its accounts of the 1998 patent settlement, the 1998 distribution buyback and the 1999 suspension of sales have no second source here, and we found no court record of the suit.[^13][^14]

notes.label: Fast Company
notes.text: The trademark sale, the scrapped machine, the 2012 acquisition and the brand’s owners rest on one article, and the owners are described as of October 2024. Who holds an ORBITZ beverage trademark today is not in our sources.[^24]

notes.label: Identity
notes.text: Science World quotes William Chalupa as a fluid-gel expert, and a William F. Chalupa is named as an inventor on the Bush Boake Allen patent. The names match; we could not confirm that they are one person. No source we opened says which patent, if any, covers Orbitz.[^9][^12]

notes.label: Also unknown
notes.text: How orbitz.com passed from the drink to the travel company; Clearly Canadian share prices for 1996 and 1997, because the filings that cover them were on paper; and its revenue for 1992 to 1997, because the secondary figures conflict.[^35]
